item.title: Trump says Nobel panel not awarding him peace prize leaves 'indelible stain' on Norway
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump lamented that the Norwegian Nobel Committee chose not to award him with its annual Peace Prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.” Speaking at a rally in Syracuse to boost New York Republicans, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having “saved more lives than anyone in history.” Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a United Nations panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza. “I’ve never heard of the person,” Trump said. “I know a lot of people. I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations, anyway. … The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.” South African lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay at the Nuremberg Forum following the announcement of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. (Daniel Karmann / Picture alliance via Getty) “And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump continued. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are antidemocracy and really enemies of civilization, and we will not forget Norway, that you didn’t give this prize with the greatest record in history.” The president added that he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his efforts because he claimed to have ended eight ongoing conflicts. The president did not mention the war in Ukraine, which has raged on through his presidency as his administration has failed to bring the conflict to an end. And in the Middle East, the president earlier this year launched an ongoing war with Iran. President Donald Trump takes the stage to speak during an election rally in Syracuse, N.Y., on Friday. (Alex Wong / Getty) Trump said the committee’s choice to award the prize to Pillay “is just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country.” Throughout his second term, the president has made clear his ambition to secure a Nobel Peace Prize, and his allies have said he deserves it for efforts to end the war in Gaza in addition to other conflicts. Earlier this year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 winner, offered to share her prize with him as she sought his support for her efforts in Venezuela after the Trump administration removed President Nicolás Maduro from power. After learning of her award at a law gathering in Germany on Friday, Pillay joked to the crowd: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” The president was in Syracuse to boost the candidacy of GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman and state Republicans. He shouted out Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for state attorney general too, before attacking sitting state Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat he has often clashed with. “And on Election Day, New Yorkers should tell both [Gov. Kathy] Hochul and that disgusting Letitia dog — she’s a dog — you’re fired, get the hell out of here.” Letitia James, New York's attorney general. (John Lamparski / Bloomberg via Getty) The Trump administration has so far failed multiple times in its efforts to prosecute James, who spearheaded an investigation into his business dealings that led to a state judge ruling he had conspired to manipulate his net worth and ordering him to pay a fine of more than $350 million. The fine was later thrown out on appeal by a state court. “Donald Trump is in Syracuse supporting the only attorney general candidate who clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, the man who ended Roe v. Wade,” a James campaign spokesperson said in response to the president’s comments. “The contrast is crystal clear and we welcome it.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/trump-says-nobel-committee-not-awarding-peace-prize-leaves-indelible-s-rcna602624

item.title: Boosting U.S. oil supplies with Russian diesel unlikely to have impact on prices, experts say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say. President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that. The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia’s war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran . The price of diesel has shattered records in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too. Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That’s because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail . Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel. That’s turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections . The president’s approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. A limited impact, at best Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally. “It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics. “If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said. And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that’s not a given. “The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe,” Lynch said. “It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it’s not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S.” If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy. However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn’t available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. “Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels,” Sternoff said. “So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them.” While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won’t have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. That’s because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted. “I don’t think it’ll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze,” he said. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/boosting-us-oil-supplies-russian-001505477.html

item.title: Trump takes lawsuit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew Chung Oct 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to ‌Russia. The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers ‌for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions. In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the ​Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida. Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims. Trump defeated Clinton in that election, despite losing the national popular vote, and served his first term in office from 2017 to 2021. US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, ‌and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller ⁠documented extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax." Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year's ⁠election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims. 'POLITICAL MANIFESTO' US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump's lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him." Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and ​his ​lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the ​sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly ‌advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts." Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories. The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions. "Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated. In court papers, lawyers for Trump and Habba have said that the decisions by the lower courts are having a "profound impact on the presidency, and the nation as a whole." Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in ‌sweeping and systematic fashion," but stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign ​conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities." Mueller said in his report that he ​found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia's effort ​to tilt the ballot in Trump's favor. Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential ‌missteps by the FBI. In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the ​FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential ​campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump's political opponents to fuel the probe. Trump's Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. ​A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor ‌who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed. Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of ​the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump's campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, ​all of which Trump denied. (Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; Editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-takes-suit-against-hillary-233623596.html

item.title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelensky for diesel prices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said. The president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure . He has also sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters. Ukrainian and European officials on Saturday reacted to Trump's diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war efforts. Diesel prices have skyrocketed due to a collision of events , including the difficulty of getting oil out of the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which has raised the price of all oil products. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted last month and published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of Iran, and blame him for higher prices. Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, “that war would have never started. There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.” Zelenskyy has “lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said. Independent estimates are that about 20% of Ukraine's territory is under Russian control. British defense officials recently estimated that about half a million Russian soldiers have been killed in the war; there are no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians have died. 20 people killed in Russian bombing in Ukraine Saturday Trump's extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday. Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days. Anger in Kyiv at Trump’s deal with Putin “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X. He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defenses, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days. Trump announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation. “Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.” For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from the central city of Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise.” “Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told The Associated Press. European allies question US-Russia deal Ukraine's European allies also expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, “as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex. The German government “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions,” spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering.” Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?” Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war. Speaking about Friday’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told AP that the Ukrainian side was not aware of the deal before the announcement. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorized to discuss the issue publicly, said Saturday the diesel deal announcement was not tied to anything under discussion in Florida. He confirmed the Ukrainian delegation had left Florida and were on their way back to Ukraine. ___ Daly reported from Washington and Morton reported from London. Associated Press journalists Bela Szandelszky in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/russian-attacks-kill-7-ukraine-071733676.html

A shooting in a residential area of Erie, Pennsylvania, left nine dead including the suspected shooter and rocked the city, police said. Authorities have released few details, though the city issued a statement that it said was intended to clear up inaccurate information that circulated following the shooting Friday. Officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter , a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots. All nine deaths occurred before officers arrived, the city said, and no additional shots were fired after that. “Sounds heard during the police response that may have been mistaken for gunfire were flash bangs associated with law enforcement's tactical response,” the city said. A news conference was scheduled for Saturday afternoon. “I have not seen anything like this in my 28-plus years,” Police Chief Rick Lorah told a local news station. “I’m not sure that the city of Erie has ever seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed.” Gov. Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin. Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh. ____ This story corrects that the total number of people found dead — nine — includes the suspected shooter. ____ Jacqueline GaNun is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. item.title: Pentagon raises official toll of troops who died during war with Iran to 21
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon acknowledged late Friday that the number of troops who have died in the Middle East during its operations against Iran is higher than previously reported, and updated the official count to include two more noncombat deaths. The Washington Post exclusively reported last month, based on information from six U.S. officials, that the numbers of service members lost was greater than what the Pentagon was reporting in its official, public database, known as the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the time called that reporting "a complete lie" in a social media post. However, late Friday, the Pentagon raised the figure publicly reported in DCAS to include additional deaths. As of Friday, the total troop deaths the administration is connecting to operations against Iran and officially reporting in DCAS stands at 21. That figure includes two additional noncombat deaths: Maj. Sorffly Davius, 46, an Army National Guard member who died in Kuwait on March 6, and an unidentified Navy suicide that occurred in September, according to a U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to provide additional context on the troop deaths. In addition, 865 service members have been wounded, according to updated data in DCAS. The military also acknowledged one additional soldier's training accident death that it said was not tied to ongoing operations against Iran. Sgt. Devin A. Seibel, 26, died during a training accident in Iraq in May. His death is now recorded in DCAS under Operation Inherent Resolve, the military's decade-long named operation against the Islamic State. That service member's death brings the total number of troops who have died in the Middle East since Feb. 28, the date that operations against Iran began, to 22. On Friday, two of the top Democratic members of the House Armed Services Committee said they were glad the Pentagon had made a "public correction" to the overall losses in the war. "There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude," the committee's top Democrat, Rep. Adam Smith (Washington) and Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (Pennsylvania), the top Democrat on the military personnel subcommittee, said in a statement, calling the fact that Congress had to get involved to have the Pentagon correct its numbers "an embarrassment" for the military. In a statement to The Post, the Pentagon did not acknowledge the changed numbers but instead said it is making further revisions to how DCAS reports casualties, including a new category of "pending adjudication" as it works through casualty reporting. The new adjudication category was first reported by Defense Scoop. The Pentagon "continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all Service member casualties," it said in a statement. It has been difficult for the public and lawmakers overseeing the Pentagon to get a clear picture of how many troops have been injured or killed during the conflict in part because the Trump administration changed mid-conflict the way it was publicly accounting for troop deaths, something critics have charged is a way for President Donald Trump to hide the true cost to military personnel. In previous conflicts those injuries or deaths - whether caused by hostile action or nonhostile causes, such as accidents or suicides - have been captured by named conflict in DCAS. In part, what has confounded DCAS data in this conflict is that earlier this year Trump declared that Operation Epic Fury had ended, even though the U.S. and Iran were still exchanging fire. In response the Pentagon created a new category of injured and killed that was not tied to Epic Fury, instead those numbers would be tallied under overseas contingency operations. item.title: Several wounded after blast at Riyadh airport as Trump weighs joining Saudi strikes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Timour Azhari and Enas Alashray RIYADH, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Several people were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday that forced a suspension of operations, the ‌country's civil aviation authority said. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, but it comes amid ‌an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis against Saudi Arabia. The airport had already been struck in two earlier attacks this week that left four ​people dead and exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's ability to defend itself as it wages war on the Houthis. Saudi Arabia's early warning system did not issue an alert ahead of Saturday's incident. The Saudi government's media office did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters. One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. ‌More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing ⁠towards the facility. An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. US TO "LOOK AT" JOINING SAUDI FIGHT AGAINST ⁠HOUTHIS: TRUMP Following the attack, US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether the United States planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, ​so we'll ​make a decision. We move very quickly," he said. The US embassy ​in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly ‌recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas." The UK and Irish embassies in Saudi Arabia said in statements on X that they were also aware of a "serious incident" at the airport. The Canadian embassy said that "ongoing military activity" had impacted operations at the airport. RIYADH DUE TO HOLD MAJOR SUMMITS Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point. Kuwait Airways said it had cancelled flights to and ‌from the Saudi capital due to what it described as the ​closure of Riyadh airport because of the "security situation" there. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways ​earlier cancelled multiple flights between their respective hubs ​and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week ‌had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend ​or cancel services to the ​Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organisers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security. The Houthis have said ​airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it ‌a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier ​this month. (Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington DC; Writing by Enas ​Alashray and Maya Gebeily;Editing by Gareth Jones and Joe Bavier) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/loud-blast-heard-riyadh-airport-141257574.html

item.title: 3 men convicted in murder of American and Australian surfers in Mexico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip when they were shot dead. Photograph: AAP The parents of Australian surfing brothers murdered in Mexico have said “no outcome can ever undo this tragedy” after three men were convicted of the 2024 killings. Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery. The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time. The judge ruled the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation. Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September. “They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.” She burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced. Speaking outside the court after the verdict, Martin Robinson thanked family and friends for their support, and also thanked the judge, court staff, the Australian embassy in Mexico and the Australian federal police. He said: “No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honouring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were. They will never be forgotten.” Debra Robinson said: “I don’t feel any different today as I did yesterday or I will tomorrow, because … Callum and Jake are not here. A verdict is a good thing, but it doesn’t bring them back.” She said she had no feelings towards the three guilty men. “I have tried to hold on to the memory of my children, my sons, and I try really not to think about them. And I don’t actually want them to have any notoriety. We don’t actually really speak their names. They’re not part of our grief really.” Martin Robinson said a foundation in their sons’ names would carry on their legacy. The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”. Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States. “The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.” Sentencing is scheduled for 16 October. The prosecution requested 210 years’ imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years. The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads. In November 2025, Ary Gisell Silva , the then-girlfriend of the main defendant, was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman , were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned. item.title: Christa Pike, who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee, is discharged from hospital
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike is out of the hospital and receiving medical care in prison following a failed execution attempt. Her legal team, Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the TN Office of the Post Conviction Defender, issued this statement on Oct. 10: "Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years. She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." More: Christa Pike's lawyers faced communication hurdles as execution failed Pike's attorneys said Oct. 8 that she'd been able to walk after spending days in the hospital unconscious and intubated following her failed execution attempt on Sept. 30. Pike's attorneys remain concerned about psychological damage and lasting impacts to her cognitive functioning. The attorneys reported they were allowed to visit with her for the first time after she regained consciousness on Oct. 6. That was after they were already told by medical professionals on Oct. 5 there was a possibility she was brain-dead and would need to be taken off life support. More: Remembering Colleen Slemmer, the teenager killed by Christa Pike On Oct. 7, they shared she was confused and angry, still badly bruised on her arms, and had pneumonia and a blood clot. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville. The day of her planned execution, last-minute legal battles caused hours of delays. After the execution was allowed to resume, Pike was given two lethal rounds of pentobarbital, which she survived. Emergency vehicles arrived as witnesses were describing what they saw and heard during the execution attempt. Gov. Bill Lee is now ordering a third-party review of what went wrong and has paused the other execution scheduled for this year. Gary Wayne Sutton had been scheduled for execution Dec. 3. The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the failed execution, said it did everything right. This article originally appeared on Nashville Tennessean: Christa Pike has been released from the hospital This article originally appeared on The Tennessean at https://www.tennessean.com/story/news/2026/10/10/christa-pike-is-out-of-the-hospitals-grateful-for-medical-care/92190155007/
